---
title: "Planning a Study: Power and Sample Size by Simulation"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5,
                      fig.align = "center")
render_start = Sys.time()
```

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(EDI)
```

Before a trial starts, someone has to answer "how many subjects do we need?" The
textbook formulas answer it for a two-sample t-test or a two-proportion z-test.
The trial you are planning may use a covariate-balancing design, a covariate-adjusted
analysis, a binary or survival outcome, or subjects who arrive one at a time. No
closed-form formula covers that combination. A simulation does: generate the trial
many times with a treatment effect you plant, run the analysis you will actually
run, and count how often it rejects.

This article walks through that workflow with EDI (Experimental Design and
Inference). It assumes you know the four steps of an EDI analysis (design, assign,
record responses, infer) from [Get started](EDI.html) or the
[continuous cookbook](cookbook-continuous.html). If you have never computed power
by simulation, Lesson 3 of
[Learn Statistics Through EDI](learn-statistics-through-edi.html) does it for a
plain t-test first.

## The recipe

1. **Fix what the trial will do.** The design (how treatment is assigned), the
   analysis (an inference class and a procedure, such as its Wald test), and the
   significance level `alpha`.
2. **Fix what you believe about the world.** An outcome model: how the covariates
   you will record relate to the outcome, how noisy the outcome is, and how the
   covariates are distributed in the population you will enroll. Then the
   effect size you want to detect, on the scale the analysis reports.
3. **Simulate.** For each candidate sample size `n`, simulate `R` trials. In each,
   draw `n` subjects, assign treatment with the design, generate outcomes with the
   planted effect, run the analysis, and record whether `p < alpha`.
4. **Read off power.** Power at `n` is the rejection rate. Pick the smallest `n`
   whose lower Monte Carlo bound clears your target (80% below). Using the lower
   bound rather than the point estimate guards against picking an `n` that only
   looks adequate because of simulation noise.
5. **Check size.** Rerun at the chosen `n` with the effect set to zero. If the
   procedure rejects much more than `alpha` of the time there, its power at that
   `n` means nothing (see [Checking size too](#checking-size-too)).

A rejection rate estimated from `R` trials has Monte Carlo standard error
$\sqrt{p(1-p)/R}$. Near the target $p = 0.8$, the number of trials needed for a
95% interval of half-width $h$ is $R = 1.96^2 \times 0.8 \times 0.2 / h^2$:

```{r reps-needed}
h = c(0.05, 0.04, 0.03, 0.02, 0.01)
data.frame(half_width = h, R_needed = ceiling(qnorm(0.975)^2 * 0.8 * 0.2 / h^2))
```

This article uses `R` = 250 to 500 per power point so that it builds in a few minutes,
which gives a half-width of 4 to 5 percentage points. For a real protocol, use
1,500 or more at the final `n`.

Two small helpers turn rejection rates into intervals and pick the `n`:

```{r helpers}
alpha = 0.05
target_power = 0.80

mc_bounds = function(p, R) {
  h = qnorm(0.975) * sqrt(p * (1 - p) / R)
  data.frame(lower = pmax(p - h, 0), upper = pmin(p + h, 1))
}

smallest_n = function(n, power, R, target = target_power) {
  ok = which(mc_bounds(power, R)$lower >= target)
  if (length(ok) == 0) NA else n[min(ok)]
}
```

## Worked example 1: a continuous outcome, two designs

**The question.** A trial will record two baseline covariates and a continuous
outcome. How many subjects are needed for 80% power to detect a treatment effect
of 0.9 outcome units at `alpha = 0.05`, under complete randomization versus
pairwise matching on the covariates?

**The outcome model.** The covariates are standard normal. The outcome depends on
them partly linearly and partly not, with residual noise of standard deviation 1:

```{r ex1-model}
draw_covariates = function(n) data.frame(x1 = rnorm(n), x2 = rnorm(n))
outcome_model = function(X) X$x1 + 0.5 * X$x2 + 0.8 * (X$x1^2 - 1) + 0.6 * X$x1 * X$x2
beta1 = 0.9          # the treatment effect to detect, in outcome units
```

**The designs and analyses.**

* `DesignFixediBCRD`: complete randomization with equal arms, analyzed with
  `InferenceContinOLS` (regression on treatment and the covariates).
* `DesignFixedBinaryMatch`: subjects are paired on Mahalanobis distance and one of
  each pair is treated. Analyzed two ways: with the same `InferenceContinOLS`, and
  with `InferenceContinKKOLSOneLik`, the matched analysis, which fits one
  covariate-adjusted regression over the within-pair differences (and any unmatched
  subjects).

### With `SimulationFramework`

[`SimulationFramework`](../reference/SimulationFramework.html) fits this job well.
It takes vectors of sample sizes `n` and effects `betaT`, runs every design against
every inference class (skipping combinations that do not apply, such as the matched
analysis on a design that does not match), and reports power per cell. Its built-in
outcome model is linear in the covariates. To use your own, pass
`custom_replication_data_generator`, a function of `(state, rep)` that returns the
covariates `X` and the control-arm mean `y_linear_model` for `state$n` subjects. For
a continuous outcome the framework then adds `betaT` to treated subjects and normal
noise with standard deviation `sd_noise`.

`inference_types_and_params = list(asymp_pval = list())` limits each analysis to its
asymptotic p-value, the fast choice for screening sample sizes. `seed` gives every
replication its own seed (`seed + i`), so the run is reproducible whatever
`num_cores` is (see [Reproducibility](reproducibility.html)).

```{r ex1-sim, message = FALSE}
ns1 = c(30L, 50L, 70L, 90L, 120L, 150L)
R1 = 250L

generator = function(state, rep) {
  X = draw_covariates(state$n)
  list(X = X, y_linear_model = outcome_model(X))
}

sim1 = SimulationFramework$new(
  response_type = "continuous",
  design_classes_and_params = list(DesignFixediBCRD = list(), DesignFixedBinaryMatch = list()),
  inference_classes_and_params = list(InferenceContinOLS = list(), InferenceContinKKOLSOneLik = list()),
  n = ns1, p = 2L, betaT = beta1, sd_noise = 1, alpha = alpha, Nrep_W = R1,
  custom_replication_data_generator = generator,
  inference_types_and_params = list(asymp_pval = list()),
  results_filename = tempfile(fileext = ".csv"), continue_from_last_result_row = FALSE,
  seed = 2026L, num_cores = 2L, verbose = FALSE
)
sim1$run()
pow1 = as.data.frame(SimulationFrameworkReport$new(sim1)$summarize())
pow1$analysis = paste(sub("^Design", "", pow1$design), "+", sub("^Inference", "", pow1$inference))
pow1 = cbind(pow1, mc_bounds(pow1$power, pow1$n_pow))
pow1[, c("n", "analysis", "power", "lower", "upper", "n_pow")]
```

```{r ex1-pick}
analyses1 = c(crd   = "FixediBCRD + ContinOLS",
              m_ols = "FixedBinaryMatch + ContinOLS",
              m_kk  = "FixedBinaryMatch + ContinKKOLSOneLik")
curve1 = lapply(analyses1, function(a) pow1[pow1$analysis == a, ][order(pow1$n[pow1$analysis == a]), ])
n_pick1 = sapply(curve1, function(d) smallest_n(d$n, d$power, d$n_pow))
n_pick1
power_at = function(curve, n) curve$power[curve$n == n]
```

```{r ex1-fig, echo = FALSE}
cols1 = c(crd = "darkorange", m_ols = "grey45", m_kk = "steelblue")
offs1 = c(crd = -1.2, m_ols = 0, m_kk = 1.2)
plot(NA, xlim = range(ns1) + c(-3, 3), ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "total sample size n",
     ylab = "power (rejection rate at alpha = 0.05)",
     main = sprintf("Power to detect an effect of %.1f, continuous outcome", beta1))
abline(h = target_power, lty = 3)
for (k in names(curve1)) {
  d = curve1[[k]]
  x = d$n + offs1[k]
  lines(x, d$power, type = "b", pch = 19, lwd = 2, col = cols1[k])
  arrows(x, d$lower, x, d$upper, angle = 90, code = 3, length = 0.03, col = cols1[k])
}
legend("bottomright", bty = "n", lwd = 2, pch = 19, col = cols1,
       legend = c("complete randomization + OLS", "matched pairs + OLS (ignores pairs)",
                  "matched pairs + matched analysis"))
```

The bars are 95% Monte Carlo intervals from `r R1` simulated trials per point, and
the dotted line is the 80% target. The smallest `n` on the grid whose lower bound
clears 80% is:

* complete randomization with OLS: **n = `r n_pick1["crd"]`** (power
  `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * power_at(curve1$crd, n_pick1["crd"]))`);
* matched pairs with the matched analysis: **n = `r n_pick1["m_kk"]`** (power
  `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * power_at(curve1$m_kk, n_pick1["m_kk"]))`);
* matched pairs analyzed with plain OLS: n = `r n_pick1["m_ols"]`.

These are provisional until the size check in [Checking size too](#checking-size-too).

So under this outcome model the matched design needs about
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * (1 - n_pick1["m_kk"] / n_pick1["crd"]))` fewer subjects
than complete randomization, for the same analysis goal. The design changed the
sample size, but only together with an analysis that uses the pairs. Plain OLS on
the matched design estimates the effect just as precisely as the matched analysis
(its mean squared error at n = `r max(ns1)` was
`r sprintf("%.3f", pow1$MSE[pow1$analysis == analyses1["m_ols"] & pow1$n == max(ns1)])`
versus
`r sprintf("%.3f", pow1$MSE[pow1$analysis == analyses1["m_kk"] & pow1$n == max(ns1)])`
for the matched analysis and
`r sprintf("%.3f", pow1$MSE[pow1$analysis == analyses1["crd"] & pow1$n == max(ns1)])`
under complete randomization), but its standard error does not know about the
matching, so it overstates the uncertainty and gives up part of the gain.

The gain depends on the outcome model. Here the covariates act on the outcome
partly through a square and an interaction, which pairing on the covariates balances
and linear adjustment does not remove. If the outcome were linear in the
covariates, OLS adjustment alone would remove most of what matching removes, and the
two designs would need similar sample sizes. That is why the outcome model is part
of the plan: change `outcome_model` to `function(X) X$x1 + 0.5 * X$x2` and rerun to
see it.

The grid is coarse. To pin the answer down, rerun with a finer grid between the last
`n` that failed and the first that passed, and more trials per point.

## Worked example 2: a binary outcome, adjusted versus unadjusted

`SimulationFramework` is convenient, but a plain loop is short and shows every step.
This example uses one.

**The question.** A binary outcome (an event occurs or not) with about a 40%
control-arm risk. Treatment lowers the log odds by 0.75. One strong continuous
prognostic covariate and one binary covariate are recorded at baseline. Under
complete randomization, how many subjects are needed for 80% power, analyzing the
risk difference with and without covariate adjustment?

```{r ex2-model}
draw_covariates2 = function(n) data.frame(x1 = rnorm(n), x2 = rbinom(n, 1, 0.4))
log_odds_control = function(X) -0.7 + 1.2 * X$x1 + 0.5 * X$x2
beta2 = -0.75        # treatment effect on the log-odds scale
```

The effect is planted on the log-odds scale, but both analyses report a risk
difference, so translate it. A large draw from the covariate distribution gives the
marginal risks the trial would see:

```{r ex2-risks}
set.seed(1)
X_big = draw_covariates2(1e6)
risk_c = mean(plogis(log_odds_control(X_big)))
risk_t = mean(plogis(log_odds_control(X_big) + beta2))
c(control = risk_c, treated = risk_t, risk_difference = risk_t - risk_c)
```

The planted effect is a drop from `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * risk_c)` to
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * risk_t)`, a risk difference of
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * (risk_t - risk_c))` percentage points. The two analyses are
`InferenceIncidGCompRiskDiff` (a logistic model with the covariates, standardized to
a marginal risk difference) and `InferenceIncidNewcombeRiskDiff` (the unadjusted
two-proportion comparison). Each simulated trial is analyzed both ways, so the two
power curves share the same trials.

```{r ex2-loop}
one_trial2 = function(n, beta, seed) {
  set.seed(seed)                                   # one seed per trial
  X = draw_covariates2(n)
  des = DesignFixediBCRD$new(n = n, response_type = "incidence", verbose = FALSE)
  des$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(X)
  des$assign_w_to_all_subjects()
  w = des$get_w()
  des$add_all_subject_responses(rbinom(n, 1, plogis(log_odds_control(X) + beta * w)))
  c(adjusted   = InferenceIncidGCompRiskDiff$new(des, verbose = FALSE)$compute_asymp_two_sided_pval(),
    unadjusted = InferenceIncidNewcombeRiskDiff$new(des, verbose = FALSE)$compute_asymp_two_sided_pval())
}

rejection_rates2 = function(n, beta, R, seed0) {
  pvals = vapply(seq_len(R), function(i) one_trial2(n, beta, seed0 + i), numeric(2))
  rowMeans(pvals < alpha)
}

ns2 = c(150L, 250L, 350L, 450L, 550L)
R2 = 500L
pow2 = t(sapply(ns2, rejection_rates2, beta = beta2, R = R2, seed0 = 0L))
rownames(pow2) = paste0("n=", ns2)
pow2
n_pick2 = apply(pow2, 2, function(p) smallest_n(ns2, p, R2))
n_pick2
```

```{r ex2-fig, echo = FALSE}
cols2 = c(adjusted = "steelblue", unadjusted = "darkorange")
offs2 = c(adjusted = -3, unadjusted = 3)
plot(NA, xlim = range(ns2) + c(-10, 10), ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "total sample size n",
     ylab = "power (rejection rate at alpha = 0.05)",
     main = sprintf("Power to detect a %.1f-point drop in risk, binary outcome",
                    100 * (risk_c - risk_t)))
abline(h = target_power, lty = 3)
for (k in colnames(pow2)) {
  b = mc_bounds(pow2[, k], R2)
  x = ns2 + offs2[k]
  lines(x, pow2[, k], type = "b", pch = 19, lwd = 2, col = cols2[k])
  arrows(x, b$lower, x, b$upper, angle = 90, code = 3, length = 0.03, col = cols2[k])
}
legend("bottomright", bty = "n", lwd = 2, pch = 19, col = cols2,
       legend = c("adjusted (g-computation risk difference)", "unadjusted (Newcombe risk difference)"))
```

With `r R2` trials per point, the smallest grid `n` whose lower bound clears 80% is
**n = `r n_pick2["adjusted"]`** for the adjusted analysis and
**n = `r n_pick2["unadjusted"]`** for the unadjusted one. At n =
`r n_pick2["adjusted"]` the adjusted analysis has power
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * pow2[paste0("n=", n_pick2["adjusted"]), "adjusted"])`
and the unadjusted one
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * pow2[paste0("n=", n_pick2["adjusted"]), "unadjusted"])`.
Here the design is fixed and the analysis changes the sample size: adjusting for a
covariate that predicts the outcome buys power for free.

The loop uses the same seeds (`seed0 + i`) at every `n`. Using common random numbers
like this makes the curves smoother than independent seeds would, since neighboring
points share much of their noise. It does not bias any single point.

## Checking size too

A power curve answers "how often does the test reject when the effect is real?" It
is only useful if the test rejects about `alpha` of the time when there is no effect.
A test that rejects 9% of the time under the null at your `n` will also look more
powerful than it is. Its "power" is partly false positives, and the sample size you
read off it is too small.

The [procedure-trust](procedure-trust.html) article explains which procedures are
valid at every sample size (exact and randomization tests) and which only as `n`
grows (Wald, likelihood-ratio, bootstrap and others). The Wald p-values used above
are in the second group, so check them by simulation at the `n` you chose: same
setup, `betaT = 0`.

For example 1, `SimulationFramework` reports `size` and an exact binomial test of it
against `alpha` (`size_pval`) when `betaT = 0`:

```{r ex1-size, message = FALSE}
R_size = 500L
sim1_null = SimulationFramework$new(
  response_type = "continuous",
  design_classes_and_params = list(DesignFixediBCRD = list(), DesignFixedBinaryMatch = list()),
  inference_classes_and_params = list(InferenceContinOLS = list(), InferenceContinKKOLSOneLik = list()),
  n = unique(as.integer(c(n_pick1["crd"], n_pick1["m_kk"]))), p = 2L, betaT = 0, sd_noise = 1,
  alpha = alpha, Nrep_W = R_size,
  custom_replication_data_generator = generator,
  inference_types_and_params = list(asymp_pval = list()),
  results_filename = tempfile(fileext = ".csv"), continue_from_last_result_row = FALSE,
  seed = 7001L, num_cores = 2L, verbose = FALSE
)
sim1_null$run()
size1 = as.data.frame(SimulationFrameworkReport$new(sim1_null)$summarize())
size1$analysis = paste(sub("^Design", "", size1$design), "+", sub("^Inference", "", size1$inference))
size1 = cbind(size1, mc_bounds(size1$size, size1$n_size))
size1 = size1[(size1$analysis == analyses1["crd"]  & size1$n == n_pick1["crd"]) |
              (size1$analysis != analyses1["crd"]  & size1$n == n_pick1["m_kk"]), ]
size1[, c("n", "analysis", "size", "lower", "upper", "size_pval")]
size_of = function(a) size1$size[size1$analysis == analyses1[a]]
row_of  = function(a) size1[size1$analysis == analyses1[a], ]
```

At the chosen sample sizes the rejection rates under no effect are
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * size_of("crd"))` (complete randomization + OLS),
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * size_of("m_kk"))` (matched analysis) and
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * size_of("m_ols"))` (plain OLS on the matched design),
each with a Monte Carlo standard error of about
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * sqrt(0.05 * 0.95 / R_size))` percentage points.

`r if (row_of("m_ols")$upper < alpha) "Plain OLS on the matched design rejects well below 5%. This is the overstated standard error seen above: the analysis is conservative, which costs power but does not invalidate it." else "Plain OLS on the matched design is not clearly below 5% here; its overstated standard error shows up mainly as lost power."`

`r kk = row_of("m_kk"); if (kk$lower > alpha) sprintf("The matched analysis is oversized at n = %d: its 95%% interval (%.1f%% to %.1f%%) lies above 5%%. Part of its %.0f%% power there is false positives, so n = %d is too small for its Wald test. Move up the grid, or use the randomization test, whose size is exact at every n.", kk$n, 100 * kk$lower, 100 * kk$upper, 100 * power_at(curve1$m_kk, kk$n), kk$n) else if (kk$size > 0.06) sprintf("The matched analysis rejects %.1f%% at n = %d (95%% interval %.1f%% to %.1f%%, exact binomial p-value %.2f against 5%%). That is above 5%%, though not clearly beyond Monte Carlo noise with %d trials. Its Wald test uses a normal reference distribution and the effective sample size of this design is the number of pairs (%d here), so some excess at this n is plausible. Before quoting n = %d in a protocol, rerun this check with more trials and confirm power and size with the randomization test at that n (see the tips below).", 100 * kk$size, kk$n, 100 * kk$lower, 100 * kk$upper, kk$size_pval, R_size, kk$n %/% 2L, kk$n) else sprintf("The matched analysis rejects %.1f%% at n = %d, close to 5%%.", 100 * kk$size, kk$n)`

For example 2, check both the chosen `n` and a small one:

```{r ex2-size}
R_size2 = 1000L
n_small = 60L
size2 = rbind(rejection_rates2(n_pick2["adjusted"], beta = 0, R = R_size2, seed0 = 1e6),
              rejection_rates2(n_small,              beta = 0, R = R_size2, seed0 = 2e6))
rownames(size2) = paste0("n=", c(n_pick2["adjusted"], n_small))
size2
small_lower = mc_bounds(size2[2, "adjusted"], R_size2)$lower
```

At n = `r n_pick2["adjusted"]` the adjusted test rejects
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * size2[1, "adjusted"])` of null trials, so its power there
can be trusted. At n = `r n_small` it rejects
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * size2[2, "adjusted"])` (lower 95% bound
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * small_lower)`, from `r R_size2` trials),
`r if (small_lower > alpha) "clearly above" else "not clearly above"` the nominal 5%.
`r if (small_lower > alpha) "A power curve for this analysis at small n would overstate what the trial can detect; a planner working at that size should switch to a randomization test, whose size is exact at every n." else "Even so, check size at your own n: the Wald test for a fitted logistic model is only asymptotically valid."`

## A sequential design

Many trials enroll subjects one at a time, and the design must assign each on
arrival. `DesignSeqOneByOneKK21` matches each new subject to an earlier unmatched one
when their covariates are close, so pairs form as the trial runs. In a simulation
the per-subject loop sits inside the per-trial loop. Here is power at the sample size
example 1 chose for the fixed matched design, with the same outcome model and effect,
analyzed by the matched class `InferenceContinKKOLSOneLik` (as in the
[continuous cookbook](cookbook-continuous.html)):

```{r seq}
one_trial_seq = function(n, beta, seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  X = draw_covariates(n)
  mu = outcome_model(X)
  des = DesignSeqOneByOneKK21$new(n = n, response_type = "continuous", verbose = FALSE)
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {                                      # subjects arrive one by one
    w_i = des$add_one_subject_to_experiment_and_assign(X[i, , drop = FALSE])
    des$add_one_subject_response(i, mu[i] + beta * w_i + rnorm(1))
  }
  InferenceContinKKOLSOneLik$new(des, verbose = FALSE)$compute_asymp_two_sided_pval()
}

n_seq = as.integer(n_pick1["m_kk"])
R_seq = 200L
p_seq = vapply(seq_len(R_seq), function(i) one_trial_seq(n_seq, beta1, 3e6 + i), numeric(1))
power_seq = mean(p_seq < alpha)
cbind(power = power_seq, mc_bounds(power_seq, R_seq))
```

At n = `r n_seq` the sequential matching design has power
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * power_seq)` (95% interval
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * mc_bounds(power_seq, R_seq)$lower)` to
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * mc_bounds(power_seq, R_seq)$upper)`, from only
`r R_seq` trials because each sequential trial is slower to simulate), against
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * power_at(curve1$m_kk, n_seq))` for the fixed matched design
that sees every subject before pairing. A sequential design cannot match as well as
one that waits for all the covariates, so expect some loss, and check the size at
your `n` as above before using the number. `SimulationFramework` also accepts
sequential design classes (its reference example runs `DesignSeqOneByOneKK21`) and
runs this per-subject loop for you.

## Practical tips

**Seeds.** Give each simulated trial its own seed, derived from its index
(`seed0 + i` above, `seed + i` inside `SimulationFramework`), rather than setting one
seed at the top and running everything in sequence. Then any single trial can be
reproduced on its own, and the results do not depend on how trials are split across
cores. [Reproducibility](reproducibility.html) explains how EDI seeds designs,
resampling and `SimulationFramework`.

**Cores.** `SimulationFramework` parallelizes over replications with `num_cores`
(this article uses 2). In your own loop, wrap the per-trial function in
`parallel::mclapply()` (Unix) or a `mirai`/`future` map, keeping the per-trial seed.
When the trials run in parallel, leave each inference object at `num_cores = 1`
so the two levels of parallelism do not compete for the same cores.

**Speed.** Screen sample sizes with asymptotic p-values, which take milliseconds.
Randomization and bootstrap p-values repeat the analysis hundreds of times per trial,
so run them only at the final `n`, to confirm the power and size of the procedure
you will report. For example:

```{r final-check, eval = FALSE}
sim_final = SimulationFramework$new(
  response_type = "continuous",
  design_classes_and_params = list(DesignFixedBinaryMatch = list()),
  inference_classes_and_params = list(InferenceContinKKOLSOneLik = list()),
  n = as.integer(n_pick1["m_kk"]), p = 2L, betaT = c(0, beta1), Nrep_W = 2000L,
  custom_replication_data_generator = generator,
  inference_types_and_params = list(asymp_pval = list(), rand_pval = list(r = 499L)),
  results_filename = "final_check.csv.bz2", seed = 2026L, num_cores = 8L
)
sim_final$run()
SimulationFrameworkReport$new(sim_final)$summarize()
```

With `results_filename` on disk and `continue_from_last_result_row = TRUE` (the
default), an interrupted run resumes where it stopped.

**Report what you assumed.** A simulated sample size is only as good as its
inputs, so the protocol should state them: the design and its settings; the analysis
class, procedure and `alpha`; the effect size and its scale (mean difference, log
odds, risk difference); the outcome model, including how strongly each covariate
predicts the outcome and the noise level or baseline risk; the covariate
distribution; the number of simulated trials per point and the resulting Monte
Carlo error; the seed; and the size check at the chosen `n`. A sensitivity run with
a weaker covariate effect or a smaller treatment effect shows how much the answer
depends on them.
